proposedNodes.task: Which strategy best addresses the new resectability problem in {patientName}'s right-hepatectomy plan?

choices.label: Right hepatectomy with middle-hepatic-vein reconstruction
choices.rationale: The intended segment IV remnant requires an outflow strategy; sufficient volume and inflow do not replace venous drainage.
choices.temptation: Global reserve and remnant size can distract from a sectoral outflow problem.
choices.counterfactual: If venous drainage were preserved but remnant reserve were insufficient, portal augmentation would address the different limitation.

choices.label: Right hepatectomy after right portal-vein embolization
choices.rationale: Portal augmentation can increase remaining liver, but does not replace venous drainage divided during resection.
choices.temptation: Treat every remnant problem as a volume problem.
choices.counterfactual: Inadequate remnant reserve with intact venous drainage could justify this strategy.

choices.label: Right hepatectomy after further conversion chemotherapy
choices.rationale: Further tumor response does not by itself provide a documented venous outlet for segment IV when the planned resection still divides it.
choices.temptation: Assume smaller tumor size resolves every technical remnant constraint.
choices.counterfactual: A tumor-clearance or vessel-involvement barrier that improves with therapy could make further conversion treatment appropriate.

proposedNodes.explanation: Follow the drainage of the tissue that will remain. Here segment IV depends on the vein included in the resection; preserving liver volume and portal inflow is insufficient. The operative assessment therefore needs an outflow reconstruction strategy. Specialist assessment must establish whether reconstruction can preserve functional drainage before the operation is approved.
reasoningSteps: Map segment IV as part of the intended remnant and identify its documented middle-hepatic-vein drainage.
Recognize that sacrificing that outflow requires a reconstruction strategy rather than further volume growth or chemotherapy under the unchanged transection plan.

The vascular map earns the new decision. Delete it and the prior HPB-referral answer cannot establish a need for reconstruction.
Patent inflow/bile ducts prevent conflating different remnant constraints; unchanged volume defeats a default volume-augmentation shortcut.

proposedNodes.task: Which investigation should be obtained next for {patientName}'s intrahepatic mass?

choices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of the intrahepatic mass
choices.rationale: Persistent indeterminacy after adequate dynamic studies requires tissue rather than accepting a tumor-specific imaging shortcut.
choices.temptation: A resident may treat any liver mass in cirrhosis as HCC or seek another surrogate marker.
choices.counterfactual: A characteristic HCC dynamic pattern in the appropriate at-risk setting could avoid a mandatory tissue step.

choices.label: Repeat dedicated multiphasic liver MRI
choices.rationale: Both current dynamic examinations are adequate and persistently atypical; repeating an unchanged acquisition does not establish histology.
choices.temptation: Mistake persistent biologic indeterminacy for a protocol problem and keep repeating scans.
choices.counterfactual: If acquisition records instead showed that the CT was portal-only and the MRI lacked contrast phases, a dedicated dynamic MRI would become appropriate.

choices.label: Serum AFP measurement
choices.rationale: AFP is not sufficiently accurate to establish or exclude HCC, and cannot resolve this persistent imaging uncertainty.
choices.temptation: Use a biomarker as a definitive diagnosis instead of resolving the atypical imaging.
choices.counterfactual: Serial AFP monitoring in an established AFP-secreting HCC is a different supported use.

proposedNodes.explanation: This is not the same problem as an unperformed dynamic acquisition. Both studies are adequate, but the tumor remains uncharacterized; tissue is needed before selecting a tumor-specific pathway. Cirrhosis does not make every liver malignancy HCC, and AFP cannot establish that diagnosis by itself.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish persistent biologic indeterminacy from the protocol inadequacy in the separate HCC case.
Choose tissue classification rather than a further staging scan or marker surrogate before tumor-specific treatment.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Treat persistently atypical findings as an unperformed protocol, or use AFP as a definitive diagnostic label.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: Adequate CT and MRI remain uncharacterizing; neither examination was omitted or technically incomplete.
proposedNodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Change the acquisition record so the outside CT was portal-only and the MRI lacked dynamic contrast phases: repeat dedicated multiphasic MRI becomes the listed key before tissue diagnosis.
deletionTest: The cirrhotic background keeps HCC a credible possibility without naming the key diagnosis.
Adequacy and actual enhancement observations distinguish this from incomplete acquisition.
Intrahepatic center preserves topic/procedure provenance; absence of an identified distant primary keeps tumor typing unresolved rather than already metastatic by supplied diagnosis.

proposedNodes.task: Which treatment assessment should be prioritized for {patientName}'s localized intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma?

choices.label: HPB assessment for margin-negative hepatic resection
choices.rationale: Localized iCCA and a preserved supplied/drained sector support margin-directed surgical assessment, including formal reserve evaluation.
choices.temptation: Classify a central hepatic malignancy as automatically requiring nonsurgical treatment.
choices.counterfactual: Uncontrolled distant progression would shift the priority to systemic assessment.

choices.label: Medical-oncology assessment for systemic cancer therapy
choices.rationale: Systemic treatment can be appropriate for unresectable or metastatic iCCA, but the current localized anatomy warrants surgical assessment rather than assuming unresectability.
choices.temptation: Treat central pedicle involvement as equivalent to uncorrectable or distant disease.
choices.counterfactual: Confirmed uncontrolled distant metastases would make this the priority.

choices.label: Interventional-radiology assessment for thermal ablation
choices.rationale: Central pedicle involvement and the need for negative-margin clearance make a focal heat-treatment shortcut inappropriate for this represented mass.
choices.temptation: Choose a focal method without interpreting the relationship to major ducts/pedicles.
choices.counterfactual: A small peripheral lesion in someone unable to undergo resection could lead to a different local-treatment assessment.

proposedNodes.explanation: The established intrahepatic histology and current spread define the disease-specific pathway; the pedicle map and liver course determine whether a negative-margin operation deserves assessment. Here HPB resection assessment is the priority, with a separate formal remnant evaluation. Systemic therapy remains relevant if staging or technical assessment later defeats complete surgery.
reasoningSteps: Read the confirmed intrahepatic histology and absence of distant disease against the involved and spared sectoral pedicles.
Combine the remaining supplied/drained sector and current hepatic course to prioritize a margin-directed surgical assessment rather than declare disease nonoperative.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Treat central pedicle involvement as automatically unresectable or choose focal heat treatment without a margin/anatomic assessment.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: Localized biopsy-proven iCCA involves central pedicles while a tumor-free supplied/drained sector remains.
proposedNodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Add confirmed uncontrolled distant metastases while retaining the local tumor map: medical-oncology systemic-treatment assessment becomes the listed key.
deletionTest: The new biopsy/staging row earns the disease-specific management decision.
Pedicle map identifies why local clearance requires an HPB operation rather than an assumed small-lesion focal procedure.
Reserve findings establish a serious operative-assessment pathway but do not prove sufficient future remnant; formal remnant evaluation remains necessary.

proposedNodes.task: Which portal branches should be embolized for {patientName}'s planned left trisectionectomy?

choices.label: Left portal and right-anterior portal branches
choices.rationale: These branches supply the planned resection territory; sparing the right-posterior portal supply directs the augmentation toward VI-VII.
choices.temptation: A resident may choose the side named by the remaining liver rather than the side being removed.
choices.counterfactual: A left hepatectomy restricted to II-IV would change the target to the left portal branch without the right-anterior branch.

choices.label: Left portal and right-posterior portal branches
choices.rationale: This sacrifices supply to VI-VII, the intended remnant, while leaving flow to resected right-anterior tissue.
choices.temptation: Confuse right anterior with right posterior or follow a side-name shortcut.
choices.counterfactual: A different resection that preserved the right-anterior sector would require a different map and could use this territory.

choices.label: Right-anterior and right-posterior portal branches
choices.rationale: Both right branches would include the remnant's portal supply, while failing to target the left resection territory.
choices.temptation: Generalize the right-portal target from a different right-hepatectomy case.
choices.counterfactual: A right hepatectomy leaving a left-sided remnant would make a right-sided target appropriate.

proposedNodes.explanation: Translate the operation into sectors before applying the embolization mechanism. The future remnant is VI-VII, supplied by the right-posterior branch. The left and right-anterior branches supply the tissue planned for removal; those are the target territories. No fixed growth interval or numeric clearance threshold is implied.
reasoningSteps: Derive the VI-VII remnant from the left-trisectionectomy resection map and match its portal branch.
Apply flow diversion to the left plus right-anterior territories while protecting remnant portal perfusion.
proposedNodes.closestCredibleError: Reuse the right-hepatectomy target or embolize the right-posterior branch that must supply the remnant.
proposedNodes.decidingObservation: The actual resection includes V/VIII as well as II-IV, while VI/VII and their portal branch remain.
proposedNodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: Change the operation to a right hepatectomy leaving II-IV: right-anterior plus right-posterior embolization becomes the listed correct target.
deletionTest: The formal reserve conclusion explains an already selected procedure; no hidden cutoff is assessed.
Resection map plus patient-specific branch map requires sectoral interpretation; the word left alone cannot select the key.
Patent remnant inflow/outflow/drainage prevents conflating an isolated growth plan with an uncorrected separate anatomic barrier.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which study should be obtained next to characterize {patientName}'s 2.6-cm liver lesion?

items.label: Ultrasound
items.value: A 2.6-cm solid liver lesion.

items.label: Outside CT protocol
items.value: Portal-venous acquisition only; arterial and delayed acquisitions were not performed.

items.label: CT observation
items.value: The lesion is lower in attenuation than the surrounding liver.

answerChoices.label: Multiphasic contrast-enhanced liver MRI
answerChoices.rationale: The outside CT did not acquire the vascular phases needed to characterize this lesion in cirrhosis.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of the lesion
answerChoices.rationale: Biopsy may become appropriate after adequate characterization remains inconclusive; the current CT was not a dynamic liver examination.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Biopsy may become appropriate after adequate characterization remains inconclusive; the current CT was not a dynamic liver examination.

answerChoices.label: Interval conventional liver ultrasound
answerChoices.rationale: A solid lesion of this size in cirrhosis needs diagnostic characterization rather than a surveillance-only repeat.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A solid lesion of this size in cirrhosis needs diagnostic characterization rather than a surveillance-only repeat.

questionDefinitions.explanation: Interpret the acquisition record before the lesion description. The portal-phase CT cannot establish the needed vascular behavior; a dedicated liver MRI supplies diagnostic contrast phases. A biopsy decision follows adequate characterization when uncertainty persists.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which diagnostic plan best fits {patientName}'s liver lesion after this MRI?

items.label: Protocol
items.value: Arterial, portal-venous and delayed contrast phases are technically adequate.

items.label: Arterial phase
items.value: Enhancement throughout the lesion exceeds background liver; it is not confined to a peripheral rim.

items.label: Portal-venous/delayed phases
items.value: The lesion becomes less enhanced than background liver, with nonperipheral washout.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with imaging-based HCC staging and treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: The represented vascular pattern in cirrhosis supports an imaging diagnosis without a mandatory tissue step.

answerChoices.label: Obtain core biopsy before HCC staging and treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: No unresolved imaging uncertainty requiring mandatory biopsy is supplied. Tissue may still be used for other specifically stated purposes.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No unresolved imaging uncertainty requiring mandatory biopsy is supplied. Tissue may still be used for other specifically stated purposes.

answerChoices.label: Obtain dynamic CT before HCC staging and treatment planning
answerChoices.rationale: A second modality is useful when the first is inconclusive; this MRI supplies an adequate characteristic pattern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A second modality is useful when the first is inconclusive; this MRI supplies an adequate characteristic pattern.

questionDefinitions.explanation: The new inference is the lesion's vascular behavior in a cirrhotic liver, not the name of a recommended test. Adequate characteristic imaging can support the HCC diagnostic pathway without mandatory biopsy. Biopsy remains possible for a separate clinical or research indication; none is supplied here.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which specialist treatment assessment should be prioritized for {patientName}'s HCC?

items.label: Tumor/staging
items.value: One peripheral 4.6-cm lesion; no major vessel involvement or extrahepatic tumor.

items.label: Observed reserve
items.value: Albumin 4.0 g/dL, bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, INR 1.0, platelets 198,000/microliter.

items.label: Clinical/endoscopic record
items.value: No ascites or encephalopathy; endoscopy shows no varices.

items.label: Resection map
items.value: A limited resection leaves most of the liver, with patent arterial/portal inflow, hepatic veins and bile ducts.

answerChoices.label: HPB-surgery assessment for hepatic resection
answerChoices.rationale: The combined reserve and anatomic observations support the existing favorable resection profile.

answerChoices.label: Transplant-center assessment for liver transplantation
answerChoices.rationale: Tumor-burden eligibility is not a requirement to choose transplantation when the patient has a favorable resection profile.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Tumor-burden eligibility is not a requirement to choose transplantation when the patient has a favorable resection profile.

answerChoices.label: Interventional-radiology assessment for thermal ablation
answerChoices.rationale: A larger peripheral lesion with favorable resection anatomy and reserve supports resection assessment here.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A larger peripheral lesion with favorable resection anatomy and reserve supports resection assessment here.

questionDefinitions.explanation: The laboratory, clinical and anatomic record must be interpreted together. They support specialist resection assessment rather than letting tumor-burden eligibility select transplantation. This is an assessment priority, not automatic clearance for an operation or an absolute prohibition of every alternative local treatment.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which treatment-planning pathway should be prioritized for {patientName} after this staging?

items.label: Tumor
items.value: A 3.6-cm hepatic HCC.

items.label: Vascular report
items.value: Tumor extends into and occludes the main portal vein; the intrahepatic arteries remain patent.

items.label: Other staging
items.value: No extrahepatic tumor identified.

items.label: Current condition
items.value: Independent in daily activities; bilirubin and INR within laboratory intervals; no ascites.

answerChoices.label: Medical-oncology assessment for systemic HCC therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Major portal tumor involvement changes the pathway despite the limited measured liver mass; preserved condition supports systemic assessment.

answerChoices.label: Interventional-radiology assessment for hepatic chemoembolization
answerChoices.rationale: Arterial embolization in a liver with major portal obstruction risks the remaining hepatic perfusion; this is not the routine favorable TACE profile.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Arterial embolization in a liver with major portal obstruction risks the remaining hepatic perfusion; this is not the routine favorable TACE profile.

answerChoices.label: Transplant-center assessment for standard HCC transplantation
answerChoices.rationale: A small measured mass does not overcome macrovascular tumor extension in a standard HCC transplant pathway.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A small measured mass does not overcome macrovascular tumor extension in a standard HCC transplant pathway.

questionDefinitions.explanation: Read vascular extension and hepatic perfusion before selecting a pathway from tumor size. Main portal occlusion makes routine arterial embolization hazardous, while macrovascular tumor extension defeats a standard small-burden transplant shortcut. Preserved hepatic function and activity support systemic-treatment assessment; this question does not rank named drugs or exclude every specialist-directed locoregional exception.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which treatment assessment should be prioritized for {patientName}'s mapped liver disease?

items.label: Current disease map
items.value: Five deep lesions in segments V-VIII and one superficial segment II lesion; all have decreased on treatment. The largest right-sided lesion measures 5.2 cm.

items.label: Other staging
items.value: No extrahepatic disease.

items.label: Surgical map
items.value: Right hepatectomy and a small segment II wedge encompass the six mapped sites. Segments II-IV otherwise contain no tumor.

items.label: Remaining liver
items.value: The planned remnant is 45% of measured liver volume; arterial/portal branches and bile ducts to it are patent. No background liver disease is documented.

answerChoices.label: HPB-surgery assessment for hepatic resection
answerChoices.rationale: The mapped sites can be encompassed by a curative-intent clearance plan with substantial remaining liver; six bilobar lesions do not independently rule it out.

answerChoices.label: Medical-oncology assessment for further systemic therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Systemic therapy remains part of multidisciplinary care, but a count-based assumption should not defer a currently plausible curative surgical assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Systemic therapy remains part of multidisciplinary care, but a count-based assumption should not defer a currently plausible curative surgical assessment.

answerChoices.label: Interventional-radiology assessment for thermal ablation
answerChoices.rationale: A large deep right-sided burden and a mapped resection pathway favor HPB assessment rather than assuming every site should undergo heat-based treatment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A large deep right-sided burden and a mapped resection pathway favor HPB assessment rather than assuming every site should undergo heat-based treatment.

questionDefinitions.explanation: Count and distribution contribute to planning, but do not independently decide resectability. This response and site map support an HPB assessment for complete liver clearance. The question does not mandate a universal perioperative chemotherapy sequence or declare systemic therapy unnecessary.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which strategy best addresses the new resectability problem in {patientName}'s right-hepatectomy plan?

items.label: Required right-sided margin
items.value: The right-sided resection must include the middle hepatic vein.

items.label: Remnant drainage map
items.value: Segment IV tributaries enter the middle hepatic vein. The left hepatic vein drains segments II-III; no segment IV connection to it is demonstrated.

items.label: Other remnant features
items.value: Left-sided arterial/portal inflow and bile ducts remain patent. The remnant volume is unchanged from the earlier plan.

answerChoices.label: Right hepatectomy with middle-hepatic-vein reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The intended segment IV remnant requires an outflow strategy; sufficient volume and inflow do not replace venous drainage.

answerChoices.label: Right hepatectomy after right portal-vein embolization
answerChoices.rationale: Portal augmentation can increase remaining liver, but does not replace venous drainage divided during resection.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Portal augmentation can increase remaining liver, but does not replace venous drainage divided during resection.

answerChoices.label: Right hepatectomy after further conversion chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Further tumor response does not by itself provide a documented venous outlet for segment IV when the planned resection still divides it.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Further tumor response does not by itself provide a documented venous outlet for segment IV when the planned resection still divides it.

questionDefinitions.explanation: Follow the drainage of the tissue that will remain. Here segment IV depends on the vein included in the resection; preserving liver volume and portal inflow is insufficient. The operative assessment therefore needs an outflow reconstruction strategy. Specialist assessment must establish whether reconstruction can preserve functional drainage before the operation is approved.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which portal territory should be embolized for {patientName}'s planned liver resection?

items.label: Tumor map after treatment
items.value: The remaining metastases are confined to segments V-VIII; segments II-IV are free of tumor.

items.label: Planned resection
items.value: Segments V-VIII. The future remnant has insufficient measured reserve for immediate resection, and the hospital team has selected portal embolization.

items.label: Portal map
items.value: Right branches supply V-VIII; the left branch supplies II-IV. The main portal trunk is patent.

answerChoices.label: Right portal branches to segments V-VIII
answerChoices.rationale: Divert portal flow from the tissue to be removed so that the tumor-free left remnant can grow.

answerChoices.label: Right portal branches and the segment IV branch
answerChoices.rationale: Segment IV belongs to the intended remnant here; including it unnecessarily removes flow from tissue being preserved.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Segment IV belongs to the intended remnant here; including it unnecessarily removes flow from tissue being preserved.

answerChoices.label: Left portal branches to segments II-IV
answerChoices.rationale: These branches supply the liver intended to remain. Embolizing them reverses the desired redistribution.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: These branches supply the liver intended to remain. Embolizing them reverses the desired redistribution.

questionDefinitions.explanation: First identify the remaining liver from the resection map, then apply the flow-diversion mechanism. The right portal territory is scheduled for removal; embolizing it promotes growth in the left remnant. The selected procedure does not guarantee that later reserve or oncologic staging will permit surgery.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which treatment plan should be prioritized for {patientName}'s colorectal cancer after portal embolization and restaging?

items.label: Remnant reassessment
items.value: The left liver has enlarged and now meets the HPB team's preoperative reserve requirement. Inflow, outflow and biliary drainage are preserved.

items.label: Restaging liver MRI
items.value: Numerous new lesions are distributed through segments II-IV as well as the known right-sided sites.

items.label: Chest restaging
items.value: Multiple new bilateral lung lesions have enlarged; a sampled lung lesion matches the colorectal primary.

answerChoices.label: Systemic-treatment reassessment with the oncology team
answerChoices.rationale: Technical reserve improved, but the new distribution and confirmed uncontrolled extrahepatic disease defeat the prior complete-clearance plan.

answerChoices.label: Proceed with the planned right hepatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The original operation would leave new metastatic disease in the remnant and lungs.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The original operation would leave new metastatic disease in the remnant and lungs.

answerChoices.label: Add left-liver ablation to the planned hepatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Local treatment of selected left-liver targets does not address this numerous new hepatic burden and enlarging bilateral lung disease without a complete plan.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Local treatment of selected left-liver targets does not address this numerous new hepatic burden and enlarging bilateral lung disease without a complete plan.

questionDefinitions.explanation: Reserve and oncologic suitability are separate requirements. The interval findings change the earlier plan despite successful remnant growth. Prioritize systemic-treatment reassessment rather than carrying the earlier hepatectomy forward; limited controlled extrahepatic disease in other patients is not declared an absolute surgical exclusion.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which study should now guide {patientName}'s liver local-treatment map?

items.label: Pretreatment liver MRI
items.value: A 2.4-cm metastasis in segment IV.

items.label: Current contrast CT
items.value: The prior segment IV site has no measurable lesion; no new liver or extrahepatic disease is identified.

items.label: Planning phase
items.value: Curative-intent local treatment has not yet been finalized.

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary-contrast liver MRI with baseline-image correlation
answerChoices.rationale: Small residual sites can remain occult on CT after treatment; hepatobiliary MRI can restore target mapping without equating radiologic disappearance with eradication.

answerChoices.label: FDG-PET/CT with baseline-image correlation
answerChoices.rationale: Metabolic staging can be useful for other questions, but it is less suited than hepatobiliary MRI to defining small post-treatment intrahepatic targets in this represented setting.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Metabolic staging can be useful for other questions, but it is less suited than hepatobiliary MRI to defining small post-treatment intrahepatic targets in this represented setting.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced liver ultrasound with baseline-image correlation
answerChoices.rationale: Ultrasound may contribute to lesion localization, especially intraoperatively, but a dedicated hepatobiliary MRI is the supported comprehensive preoperative map here.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Ultrasound may contribute to lesion localization, especially intraoperatively, but a dedicated hepatobiliary MRI is the supported comprehensive preoperative map here.

questionDefinitions.explanation: Compare the current image with the original metastatic site. Disappearance on CT is not proof of sterilization; hepatobiliary-contrast MRI can detect a small residual target and refine the operative map. This does not settle the separate question of how to treat a site that remains occult on both high-quality MRI and intraoperative ultrasound.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s reidentified segment IV metastasis after restaging?

items.label: Segment IV site
items.value: A 1.2-cm lesion is again visible at the original metastatic location.

items.label: Local relationship
items.value: The lesion is 3 mm from the left hepatic duct; the duct wall is not invaded.

items.label: Remaining liver
items.value: No other lesions are identified. The portal branches and major hepatic veins are patent; the HPB map supports a limited parenchymal resection.

answerChoices.label: Limited resection of the segment IV lesion
answerChoices.rationale: The isolated recovered lesion is suitable for local clearance, but its central-duct proximity constrains thermal treatment.

answerChoices.label: Microwave ablation of the segment IV lesion
answerChoices.rationale: Heat immediately beside the central left duct risks biliary injury despite the small tumor diameter.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Heat immediately beside the central left duct risks biliary injury despite the small tumor diameter.

answerChoices.label: Further systemic therapy for the hepatic metastasis
answerChoices.rationale: A currently isolated reidentified site with a local-clearance map warrants local treatment planning; further drugs do not resolve the central-duct constraint or automatically replace local clearance.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A currently isolated reidentified site with a local-clearance map warrants local treatment planning; further drugs do not resolve the central-duct constraint or automatically replace local clearance.

questionDefinitions.explanation: Small diameter does not settle local treatment. The reidentified metastasis lies immediately beside the left hepatic duct, while the supplied map supports limited resection and no other disease is identified. That favors local clearance by resection among these plans. No universal resection-over-ablation superiority or routine stop-chemotherapy rule is asserted.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which investigation should be obtained next for {patientName}'s intrahepatic mass?

items.label: Mass
items.value: A 4.4-cm mass centered in segment IV, extending toward the left and right-anterior pedicles.

items.label: Completed imaging
items.value: Both dedicated multiphasic CT and contrast MRI have adequate vascular phases.

items.label: Observed enhancement
items.value: Peripheral enhancement with progressive delayed central enhancement on both studies.

items.label: Other imaging
items.value: No extrahepatic mass or metastasis is identified. The extrahepatic bile duct is not the center of the lesion.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of the intrahepatic mass
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent indeterminacy after adequate dynamic studies requires tissue rather than accepting a tumor-specific imaging shortcut.

answerChoices.label: Repeat dedicated multiphasic liver MRI
answerChoices.rationale: Both current dynamic examinations are adequate and persistently atypical; repeating an unchanged acquisition does not establish histology.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Both current dynamic examinations are adequate and persistently atypical; repeating an unchanged acquisition does not establish histology.

answerChoices.label: Serum AFP measurement
answerChoices.rationale: AFP is not sufficiently accurate to establish or exclude HCC, and cannot resolve this persistent imaging uncertainty.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: AFP is not sufficiently accurate to establish or exclude HCC, and cannot resolve this persistent imaging uncertainty.

questionDefinitions.explanation: This is not the same problem as an unperformed dynamic acquisition. Both studies are adequate, but the tumor remains uncharacterized; tissue is needed before selecting a tumor-specific pathway. Cirrhosis does not make every liver malignancy HCC, and AFP cannot establish that diagnosis by itself.

questionDefinitions.stem: Which treatment assessment should be prioritized for {patientName}'s localized intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma?

items.label: Tissue and staging
items.value: The tumor is confirmed as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; completed evaluation identifies no extrahepatic primary or distant tumor.

items.label: Anatomic report

answerChoices.rationale: Small residual sites can remain occult on CT after treatment; hepatobiliary MRI can restore target mapping without equating radiologic disappearance with eradication.

answerChoices.label: Interval conventional liver ultrasound

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the acquisition record before the lesion description. The portal-phase CT cannot establish the needed vascular behavior; a dedicated liver MRI supplies diagnostic contrast phases. A biopsy decision follows adequate characterization when uncertainty persists.

decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment-planning pathway should be prioritized for {patientName} after this staging?

answerChoices.label: Medical-oncology assessment for systemic HCC therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Major portal tumor involvement changes the pathway despite the limited measured liver mass; preserved condition supports systemic assessment.

answerChoices.label: Interventional-radiology assessment for hepatic chemoembolization
answerChoices.rationale: Arterial embolization in a liver with major portal obstruction risks the remaining hepatic perfusion; this is not the routine favorable TACE profile.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read vascular extension and hepatic perfusion before selecting a pathway from tumor size. answerChoices.label: HPB-surgery assessment for hepatic resection
answerChoices.rationale: The mapped sites can be encompassed by a curative-intent clearance plan with substantial remaining liver; six bilobar lesions do not independently rule it out.

answerChoices.label: Medical-oncology assessment for further systemic therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Systemic therapy remains part of multidisciplinary care, but a count-based assumption should not defer a currently plausible curative surgical assessment.

answerChoices.label: Interventional-radiology assessment for thermal ablation
answerChoices.rationale: A large deep right-sided burden and a mapped resection pathway favor HPB assessment rather than assuming every site should undergo heat-based treatment.

decisionNodes.explanation: Count and distribution contribute to planning, but do not independently decide resectability. This response and site map support an HPB assessment for complete liver clearance. The question does not mandate a universal perioperative chemotherapy sequence or declare systemic therapy unnecessary.

items.label: Current disease map
items.value: Five deep lesions in segments V-VIII and one superficial segment II lesion; all have decreased on treatment. The largest right-sided lesion measures 5.2 cm.

items.label: Other staging
items.value: No extrahepatic disease.

items.label: Surgical map
items.value: Right hepatectomy and a small segment II wedge encompass the six mapped sites. Segments II-IV otherwise contain no tumor.

items.label: Remaining liver
items.value: The planned remnant is 45% of measured liver volume; arterial/portal branches and bile ducts to it are patent. No background liver disease is documented.

decisionNodes.stem: Which strategy best addresses the new resectability problem in {patientName}'s right-hepatectomy plan?

answerChoices.label: Right hepatectomy with middle-hepatic-vein reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The intended segment IV remnant requires an outflow strategy; sufficient volume and inflow do not replace venous drainage.

answerChoices.label: Right hepatectomy after right portal-vein embolization
answerChoices.rationale: Portal augmentation can increase remaining liver, but does not replace venous drainage divided during resection.

answerChoices.label: Right hepatectomy after further conversion chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Further tumor response does not by itself provide a documented venous outlet for segment IV when the planned resection still divides it.

decisionNodes.explanation: Follow the drainage of the tissue that will remain. Here segment IV depends on the vein included in the resection; preserving liver volume and portal inflow is insufficient. The operative assessment therefore needs an outflow reconstruction strategy. Specialist assessment must establish whether reconstruction can preserve functional drainage before the operation is approved.

items.label: Required right-sided margin
items.value: The right-sided resection must include the middle hepatic vein.

items.label: Remnant drainage map
items.value: Segment IV tributaries enter the middle hepatic vein. The left hepatic vein drains segments II-III; no segment IV connection to it is demonstrated.

items.label: Other remnant features
items.value: Left-sided arterial/portal inflow and bile ducts remain patent. The remnant volume is unchanged from the earlier plan.

decisionNodes.stem: Which portal territory should be embolized for {patientName}'s planned liver resection?

answerChoices.label: Right portal branches to segments V-VIII
answerChoices.rationale: Divert portal flow from the tissue to be removed so that the tumor-free left remnant can grow.

answerChoices.label: Right portal branches and the segment IV branch
answerChoices.rationale: Segment IV belongs to the intended remnant here; including it unnecessarily removes flow from tissue being preserved.

answerChoices.label: Left portal branches to segments II-IV
answerChoices.rationale: These branches supply the liver intended to remain. Embolizing them reverses the desired redistribution.

decisionNodes.explanation: First identify the remaining liver from the resection map, then apply the flow-diversion mechanism. The right portal territory is scheduled for removal; embolizing it promotes growth in the left remnant. The selected procedure does not guarantee that later reserve or oncologic staging will permit surgery.

items.label: Tumor map after treatment
items.value: The remaining metastases are confined to segments V-VIII; segments II-IV are free of tumor.

items.label: Planned resection
items.value: Segments V-VIII. The future remnant has insufficient measured reserve for immediate resection, and the hospital team has selected portal embolization.

items.label: Portal map
items.value: Right branches supply V-VIII; the left branch supplies II-IV. The main portal trunk is patent.

answerChoices.rationale: Technical reserve improved, but the new distribution and confirmed uncontrolled extrahepatic disease defeat the prior complete-clearance plan.

answerChoices.rationale: The original operation would leave new metastatic disease in the remnant and lungs.

answerChoices.label: Add left-liver ablation to the planned hepatectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Local treatment of selected left-liver targets does not address this numerous new hepatic burden and enlarging bilateral lung disease without a complete plan.

decisionNodes.stem: Which study should now guide {patientName}'s liver local-treatment map?

answerChoices.label: Hepatobiliary-contrast liver MRI with baseline-image correlation
answerChoices.rationale: Small residual sites can remain occult on CT after treatment; hepatobiliary MRI can restore target mapping without equating radiologic disappearance with eradication.

answerChoices.label: FDG-PET/CT with baseline-image correlation
answerChoices.rationale: Metabolic staging can be useful for other questions, but it is less suited than hepatobiliary MRI to defining small post-treatment intrahepatic targets in this represented setting.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced liver ultrasound with baseline-image correlation
answerChoices.rationale: Ultrasound may contribute to lesion localization, especially intraoperatively, but a dedicated hepatobiliary MRI is the supported comprehensive preoperative map here.

decisionNodes.explanation: Compare the current image with the original metastatic site. Disappearance on CT is not proof of sterilization; hepatobiliary-contrast MRI can detect a small residual target and refine the operative map. This does not settle the separate question of how to treat a site that remains occult on both high-quality MRI and intraoperative ultrasound.

items.label: Pretreatment liver MRI
items.value: A 2.4-cm metastasis in segment IV.

items.label: Current contrast CT
items.value: The prior segment IV site has no measurable lesion; no new liver or extrahepatic disease is identified.

items.label: Planning phase
items.value: Curative-intent local treatment has not yet been finalized.

decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s reidentified segment IV metastasis after restaging?

answerChoices.label: Limited resection of the segment IV lesion
answerChoices.rationale: The isolated recovered lesion is suitable for local clearance, but its central-duct proximity constrains thermal treatment.

answerChoices.label: Microwave ablation of the segment IV lesion
answerChoices.rationale: Heat immediately beside the central left duct risks biliary injury despite the small tumor diameter.

answerChoices.label: Further systemic therapy for the hepatic metastasis
answerChoices.rationale: A currently isolated reidentified site with a local-clearance map warrants local treatment planning; further drugs do not resolve the central-duct constraint or automatically replace local clearance.

decisionNodes.explanation: Small diameter does not settle local treatment. The reidentified metastasis lies immediately beside the left hepatic duct, while the supplied map supports limited resection and no other disease is identified. That favors local clearance by resection among these plans. No universal resection-over-ablation superiority or routine stop-chemotherapy rule is asserted.

items.label: Segment IV site
items.value: A 1.2-cm lesion is again visible at the original metastatic location.

items.label: Local relationship
items.value: The lesion is 3 mm from the left hepatic duct; the duct wall is not invaded.

items.label: Remaining liver
items.value: No other lesions are identified. The portal branches and major hepatic veins are patent; the HPB map supports a limited parenchymal resection.

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should be obtained next for {patientName}'s intrahepatic mass?

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of the intrahepatic mass
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent indeterminacy after adequate dynamic studies requires tissue rather than accepting a tumor-specific imaging shortcut.

answerChoices.label: Repeat dedicated multiphasic liver MRI
answerChoices.rationale: Both current dynamic examinations are adequate and persistently atypical; repeating an unchanged acquisition does not establish histology.

answerChoices.label: Serum AFP measurement
answerChoices.rationale: AFP is not sufficiently accurate to establish or exclude HCC, and cannot resolve this persistent imaging uncertainty.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is not the same problem as an unperformed dynamic acquisition. Both studies are adequate, but the tumor remains uncharacterized; tissue is needed before selecting a tumor-specific pathway. Cirrhosis does not make every liver malignancy HCC, and AFP cannot establish that diagnosis by itself.

items.label: Mass
items.value: A 4.4-cm mass centered in segment IV, extending toward the left and right-anterior pedicles.

items.label: Completed imaging
items.value: Both dedicated multiphasic CT and contrast MRI have adequate vascular phases.

items.label: Observed enhancement
items.value: Peripheral enhancement with progressive delayed central enhancement on both studies.

items.label: Other imaging
items.value: No extrahepatic mass or metastasis is identified. The extrahepatic bile duct is not the center of the lesion.

decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment assessment should be prioritized for {patientName}'s localized intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma?

answerChoices.label: HPB assessment for margin-negative hepatic resection
answerChoices.rationale: Localized iCCA and a preserved supplied/drained sector support margin-directed surgical assessment, including formal reserve evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Medical-oncology assessment for systemic cancer therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Systemic treatment can be appropriate for unresectable or metastatic iCCA, but the current localized anatomy warrants surgical assessment rather than assuming unresectability.

answerChoices.label: Interventional-radiology assessment for thermal ablation
answerChoices.rationale: Central pedicle involvement and the need for negative-margin clearance make a focal heat-treatment shortcut inappropriate for this represented mass.

decisionNodes.explanation: The established intrahepatic histology and current spread define the disease-specific pathway; the pedicle map and liver course determine whether a negative-margin operation deserves assessment. Here HPB resection assessment is the priority, with a separate formal remnant evaluation. Systemic therapy remains relevant if staging or technical assessment later defeats complete surgery.

items.label: Tissue and staging
items.value: The tumor is confirmed as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; completed evaluation identifies no extrahepatic primary or distant tumor.

items.label: Anatomic report

caseDefinitions.learningSummary: This is not the same problem as an unperformed dynamic acquisition. Both studies are adequate, but the tumor remains uncharacterized; tissue is needed before selecting a tumor-specific pathway. Cirrhosis does not make every liver malignancy HCC, and AFP cannot establish that diagnosis by itself. The established intrahepatic histology and current spread define the disease-specific pathway; the pedicle map and liver course determine whether a negative-margin operation deserves assessment. Here HPB resection assessment is the priority, with a separate formal remnant evaluation. Systemic therapy remains relevant if staging or technical assessment later defeats complete surgery. Translate the operation into sectors before applying the embolization mechanism. The future remnant is VI-VII, supplied by the right-posterior branch. The left and right-anterior branches supply the tissue planned for removal; those are the target territories. No fixed growth interval or numeric clearance threshold is implied.

decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment-planning pathway should be prioritized for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Transplant-center assessment for liver transplantation
answerChoices.rationale: The tumor burden supports transplant assessment, while the raw decompensation/portal-hypertension findings prevent treating the small tumor as a favorable routine-resection profile.

answerChoices.label: HPB-surgery assessment for partial liver resection
answerChoices.rationale: A solitary small lesion makes resection attractive, but the represented liver course is outside the supported favorable compensated-resection profile.

answerChoices.label: Interventional-radiology assessment for liver ablation
answerChoices.rationale: Local tumor control can be part of specialist care, but a tumor-only pathway does not replace the transplant assessment supported by the combined burden and decompensated liver findings.

decisionNodes.explanation: First apply the tumor-burden and spread findings, then assess the liver separately. This course supports transplant-center assessment rather than assuming that a small solitary HCC makes partial hepatectomy suitable. Assessment is not guaranteed listing, and locoregional treatment may be considered within specialist planning.

ownerApprovals.evidenceBoundary: All 13 current exact drafts, new concepts, claim applications and finite contexts remain needs_clinician_review; no new independent PASS or manager acceptance.
ownerApprovals.decisionNeeded: Clinically sign off or return the exact versions and their mapped claims after independent review; do not inherit historical approvals.

ownerApprovals.competingActions: Middle-hepatic-vein reconstruction strategy versus right portal augmentation or additional conversion chemotherapy.
ownerApprovals.evidenceBoundary: Sources require preserved remnant outflow; they do not independently establish technical reconstructibility for every anatomy. This is a constructed operative planning map.
ownerApprovals.decisionNeeded: Does the supplied sectoral map support this reconstruction-strategy question as the single best plan, or should it be narrowed to an HPB outflow-planning assessment?

ownerApprovals.competingActions: Systemic assessment versus routine TACE or standard HCC transplant assessment.
ownerApprovals.evidenceBoundary: NCI supports the portal-flow safety concern and active systemic pathway; current full AASLD update not newly retrieved. Specialized Y90/TARE exceptions are outside these options.
ownerApprovals.decisionNeeded: Confirm that the main-portal tumor-occlusion scenario supports the proposed priority without implying that all locoregional therapy is prohibited.

ownerApprovals.competingActions: Hepatobiliary MRI versus PET/contrast ultrasound; limited resection versus microwave ablation or further systemic treatment.
ownerApprovals.evidenceBoundary: Post-treatment mapping evidence is observational; central-duct injury principle is supported, but exact limited resection feasibility needs clinical review. Truly occult-site treatment and universal ablation-versus-resection rules are withheld.
ownerApprovals.decisionNeeded: Confirm MRI priority and the specific duct-adjacent resection map; preserve the withheld blind-resection-versus-surveillance controversy.

ownerApprovals.competingActions: Biopsy versus repeat dynamic MRI/AFP; margin-directed HPB assessment versus systemic/ablation assessment; named embolization territories.
ownerApprovals.evidenceBoundary: One government summary directly supports localized iCCA resection and augmentation; no independent current iCCA guideline retrieved. No node-count, transplant-protocol or fixed FLR rule authored.
ownerApprovals.decisionNeeded: Confirm the atypical-imaging tissue step, margin-directed assessment and left-trisectionectomy portal map for this exact clinical course.

ownerApprovals.competingActions: Current numeric/interval, node-dissection, regimen, transplant-policy and truly occult-site management alternatives listed in withheldTeachingPoints.
ownerApprovals.evidenceBoundary: Six explicit new teaching-point holds; no key has been created for them.
ownerApprovals.decisionNeeded: Maintain holds until permitted full sources and a named clinical decision resolve the exact boundary.

reviewDecision.title: Nora Patel: characterize a lesion after an incomplete CT acquisition
fairness: Multiphasic liver MRI is the best offered next investigation. The resident must distinguish an incomplete acquisition from a completed but indeterminate examination, then combine lesion size and cirrhosis with that distinction to choose diagnostic imaging over surveillance or immediate biopsy.

The record explicitly says the phases were not performed; it does not confuse missing exported images with missing acquisition. This necessary observation should remain. The phase vocabulary is medically relevant rather than an unfair key-only lexical match.
The presentation, exhibit and task are sufficient without a previous node. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally strong offered alternative was identified.

Review-wide limitation: this is an offline editorial and clinical-reasoning review of the candidate visible text, not fresh source verification or clinical sign-off. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured performance or verified exam frequencies. Every candidate remains needs_clinician_review, including editorial PASS items. Retained, retired/replaced-by-existing, parked and withheld records were not reassessed. Runtime randomization, rendering and wait metadata were outside this visible-text review.
suggestions: Retain the actual acquisition record and the complete separated task. Do not add dynamic CT as another choice without a patient-specific reason to prefer MRI; it could create a second defensible answer.
Keep the explanation focused on acquisition adequacy. Do not expand it to state the next node's exact diagnostic criterion or keyed disposition.

reviewDecision.title: Elaine Brooks: resection versus transplantation or ablation
fairness: Resection assessment is the best offered priority for this solitary peripheral tumor with preserved synthetic function, no supplied clinical evidence of significant portal hypertension, and a limited resection map. The tumor burden also makes transplant referral a plausible resident error rather than a random foil.

The resident must interpret reserve and portal-hypertension observations, then integrate tumor size and operative anatomy to rank the three treatments. The 4.6-cm size makes thermal ablation a less attractive competitor without inventing a new numerical rule.

The resection map is decision-critical feasibility information, not a sufficient answer by itself: poor reserve or portal hypertension could still change the priority. The three options name concrete treatments at the same assessment stage.

The explanation appropriately limits the answer to assessment rather than operative clearance. This standalone item is coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally strong offered priority was identified; current guideline confirmation remains outside this offline review.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between tumor-burden eligibility and the best initial treatment assessment. Do not turn the explanation into a universal claim that transplantation or ablation is prohibited.
Preserve the raw reserve and portal-hypertension findings rather than replacing them with a resection-eligible label.

reviewDecision.title: Omar Bennett: HCC with main portal-vein tumor occlusion
fairness: Medical-oncology assessment for systemic therapy is the best offered pathway. Macrovascular tumor extension changes the interpretation of an otherwise small tumor, and main portal occlusion creates a separate perfusion concern for routine chemoembolization.

The resident must interpret the vascular staging and then use portal perfusion plus preserved function/activity to rank systemic therapy, chemoembolization and standard transplantation. Patent hepatic arteries can tempt an embolization choice but do not resolve the portal-flow problem.

The supplied HCC diagnosis is legitimate for this management task. The word standard appropriately bounds the transplant comparison; it is not a rhetorical absolute or an independent nonmedical route to the key.

The explanation preserves the distinction between routine chemoembolization and specialist locoregional exceptions. This standalone case is coherent, and no confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. Exact current systemic regimens and selected-center exceptions were not verified offline.
suggestions: Keep the explicit tumor nature of the portal occlusion; changing it to an unspecified thrombus would materially change the staging inference.
Retain the limited claim about routine chemoembolization and standard transplantation rather than generalizing to all arterial treatments or all transplant protocols.

Reserve and oncologic clearance are separate questions. New widespread hepatic and biopsy-confirmed pulmonary progression supports systemic reassessment. Selected limited extrahepatic disease need not exclude every local approach, but the current record does not describe that limited, completely treatable setting.
Current progression in both the intended remnant and multiple pulmonary sites defeats the prior liver-only clearance plan despite improved reserve.
If restaging instead showed only completely treatable limited disease with suitable reserve, a complete local-clearance assessment could be reasonable.
The supplied widespread progression makes this a weak competitor without additional evidence of a feasible comprehensive clearance plan. Limited extrahepatic disease is a different situation.
Limited controlled hepatic and pulmonary disease with all sites amenable to complete treatment could support this assessment.
This ignores established progressive pulmonary disease and is not a close treatment-priority competitor. Improved remnant function does not resolve the disease-distribution problem.
If no extrahepatic disease existed and every hepatic site were locally treatable with sufficient reserve, this pathway could be assessed.
Review the current extent and progression of both hepatic and extrahepatic disease rather than relying on a prior liver-only operative map.
Separate adequate reserve from complete oncologic clearance; the former does not rescue a plan that cannot address the current distribution.

candidate.task: Which plan best reconciles {patientName}'s embolization request with the current operative documentation?

choices.label: Reconcile the intended resection before assigning embolization targets
choices.rationale: The documents specify different possible retained territories. The intended operation and its reserve assessment must be reconciled before one target set can be justified.
choices.temptation: The new discrepancy is real, but a request cannot safely define the final territory when operative intent is unresolved.
choices.counterfactual: A confirmed updated operation and reserve map would permit its corresponding target set to be selected.

choices.counterfactual: If a completed updated review confirmed the extended operation and adequate posterior preparation pathway, this target set could fit.

finiteProfilesReviewed.presentation: {patientName}, a 63-year-old woman with compensated cirrhosis, comes to clinic to review outside studies of an intrahepatic mass.

priorVisibleFeedback: The imaging characterizes this as a suspicious malignant mass but does not establish its histologic identity. Rim arterial enhancement with progressive central enhancement is not the characteristic HCC pattern. In this cirrhotic-liver diagnostic pathway, obtain core tissue before choosing tumor-specific treatment. This is not a rule that every potentially resectable cholangiocarcinoma requires preoperative biopsy.

First derive the remnant from tumor clearance: left plus right-anterior pedicle involvement leaves the posterior VI-VII territory after the proposed extended resection. Its measured 14% is far below a conservative remnant-volume boundary, and cirrhosis adds functional concern despite normal whole-liver tests. Prioritize augmentation planning with repeat volume/function and oncologic assessment. This preserves a possible surgical pathway without declaring the current operation safe or guaranteeing that augmentation will permit resection.

items.value: Dedicated multiphasic CT and contrast MRI both have technically adequate arterial, portal-venous and delayed phases.

items.value: 4.4-cm intrahepatic segment IV mass extending toward left and right-anterior pedicles. Arterial enhancement is confined to a peripheral rim, followed by progressive delayed central enhancement.

items.label: Staging and access
items.value: No extrahepatic primary or metastasis on current staging. The mass is not centered on an extrahepatic duct. Image-guided core sampling is feasible.

priorVisibleNodes.task: Which diagnostic plan should guide selection of tumor-specific treatment for {patientName}'s intrahepatic mass?

choices.label: Obtain core biopsy before selecting tumor-specific treatment
choices.rationale: The rim-enhancing malignant pattern does not establish HCC histology in this cirrhotic liver. AASLD recommends tissue classification for this nonspecific malignant pattern when biopsy is feasible.

choices.label: Use current imaging to select HCC-directed treatment
choices.rationale: The current pattern lacks the characteristic HCC combination. Selecting an HCC-specific treatment pathway from cirrhosis plus a liver mass would skip the unresolved tumor-type decision.

choices.label: Obtain contrast ultrasound before deciding on tissue sampling
choices.rationale: Another imaging discriminator does not replace recommended tissue classification for this malignant nonspecific pattern when adequate CT/MRI and feasible biopsy are already available.
